Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,

automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# statix

> Lints and suggestions for the Nix programming language.

`statix check` highlights antipatterns in Nix code. `statix
fix` can fix several such occurrences.

For the time-being, `statix` works only with ASTs
produced by the `rnix-parser` crate and does not evaluate
any nix code (imports, attr sets etc.).

## Examples

```shell
$ statix check tests/c.nix
[W04] Warning: Assignment instead of inherit from
   ╭─[tests/c.nix:2:3]
   │
 2 │   mtl = pkgs.haskellPackages.mtl;
   ·   ───────────────┬───────────────
   ·                  ╰───────────────── This assignment is better written with inherit
───╯

$ statix fix --dry-run tests/c.nix
--- tests/c.nix
+++ tests/c.nix [fixed]
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 let
-  mtl = pkgs.haskellPackages.mtl;
+  inherit (pkgs.haskellPackages) mtl;
 in
 null
```

## Installation

`statix` is available via a nix flake:

```shell
architecture
============

statix has the following components:
  * bin: the CLI/entrypoint
  * lib: library of lints and utilities to define these lints
  * vfs: virtual filesystem
  * macros: procedural macros to help define a lint


bin
---

This is the main point of interaction between `statix` and
the end user. It's output is human-readable and should also
support JSON/errorfmt outputs for external tools to use.


lib
---

A library of AST-based lints and utilities to help write
those lints. It should be easy for newcomers to write lints
without being familiar with the rest of the codebase.


vfs
---

VFS is an in-memory filesystem. It provides cheap-to-copy
handles (`FileId`s) to access paths and file contents.


macros
------

This crate intends to be a helper layer to declare lints and
their metadata.
VFS
---
- do all the IO in one place
- pass file handles around

Interface
---------
- load files to be read as VFS
- path interner
- traits to go from Report to text/errfmt
- offline documentation/explaination for lints

Fix
---
- multipass runner with hare & tortoise for cycle detection
- fix all possible suggestions
- work with a config generated by CLI
- read data from VFS
- produce a Report

Analysis
--------
- work with a config generated by CLI
- read data from VFS
- produce a Report

Tests
-----
- figure out a way to generate stable singleline output for
  analysis tests
- use stderr tests for fixes

Lint ideas
----------
- unused let bindings
- unused rec
- invalid or potentially risky string interpolations
- useless parens in infix exprs
- unused function params
- manual map over list
- merge inherit
- merge inherit-from
- empty inherit
- useless antiquote/splice (where is antiquote truly
  required?)
- useless variadic (things like `{...} : expr`, replace with
  `_: expr`)
- redundant pattern `{...} @ inputs : expr`, replace with
  `inputs: expr`
- useless hasAttr: `if x ? a then x.a else default` can be
  replaced with `x.a or default`

Extensions
----------
- vim plugin to populate location list with errors

## What it does
Checks for expressions of the form `x == true`, `x != true` and
suggests using the variable directly.

## Why is this bad?
Unnecessary code.

## Example
Instead of checking the value of `x`:

```nix
if x == true then 0 else 1
```

Use `x` directly:

```nix
if x then 0 else 1
```
## What it does
Checks for `let-in` expressions which create no new bindings.

## Why is this bad?
`let-in` expressions that create no new bindings are useless.
These are probably remnants from debugging or editing expressions.

## Example

```nix
let in pkgs.statix
```

Preserve only the body of the `let-in` expression:

```nix
pkgs.statix
```
## What it does
Checks for bindings of the form `a = a`.

## Why is this bad?
If the aim is to bring attributes from a larger scope into
the current scope, prefer an inherit statement.

## Example

```nix
let
  a = 2;
in
  { a = a; b = 3; }
```

Try `inherit` instead:

```nix
let
  a = 2;
in
  { inherit a; b = 3; }
```
## What it does
Checks for bindings of the form `a = someAttr.a`.

## Why is this bad?
If the aim is to extract or bring attributes of an attrset into
scope, prefer an inherit statement.

## Example

```nix
let
  mtl = pkgs.haskellPackages.mtl;
in
  null
```

Try `inherit` instead:

```nix
let
  inherit (pkgs.haskellPackages) mtl;
in
  null
```
## What it does
Checks for legacy-let syntax that was never formalized.

## Why is this bad?
This syntax construct is undocumented, refrain from using it.

## Example

Legacy let syntax makes use of an attribute set annotated with
`let` and expects a `body` attribute.
```nix
let {
  body = x + y;
  x = 2;
  y = 3;
}
```

This is trivially representible via `rec`, which is documented
and more widely known:

```nix
rec {
  body = x + y;
  x = 2;
  y = 3;
}.body
```
## What it does
Checks for `let-in` expressions whose body is another `let-in`
expression.

## Why is this bad?
Unnecessary code, the `let-in` expressions can be merged.

## Example

```nix
let
  a = 2;
in
let
  b = 3;
in
  a + b
```

Merge both `let-in` expressions:

```nix
let
  a = 2;
  b = 3;
in
  a + b
```
## What it does
Checks for eta-reducible functions, i.e.: converts lambda
expressions into free standing functions where applicable.

## Why is this bad?
Oftentimes, eta-reduction results in code that is more natural
to read.

## Example

```nix
let
  double = i: 2 * i;
in
map (x: double x) [ 1 2 3 ]
```

The lambda passed to the `map` function is eta-reducible, and the
result reads more naturally:

```nix
let
  double = i: 2 * i;
in
map double [ 1 2 3 ]
```
## What it does
Checks for unnecessary parentheses.

## Why is this bad?
Unnecessarily parenthesized code is hard to read.

## Example

```nix
let
  double = (x: 2 * x);
  ls = map (double) [ 1 2 3 ];
in
  (2 + 3)
```

Remove unnecessary parentheses:

```nix
let
  double = x: 2 * x;
  ls = map double [ 1 2 3 ];
in
  2 + 3
```
## What it does
Checks for an empty variadic pattern: `{...}`, in a function
argument.

## Why is this bad?
The intention with empty patterns is not instantly obvious. Prefer
an underscore identifier instead, to indicate that the argument
is being ignored.

## Example

```nix
client = { ... }: {
  services.irmaseal-pkg.enable = true;
};
```

Replace the empty variadic pattern with `_` to indicate that you
intend to ignore the argument:

```nix
client = _: {
  services.irmaseal-pkg.enable = true;
};
```
## What it does
Checks for binds of the form `inputs @ { ... }` in function
arguments.

## Why is this bad?
The variadic pattern here is redundant, as it does not capture
anything.

## Example

```nix
inputs @ { ... }: inputs.nixpkgs
```

Remove the pattern altogether:

```nix
inputs: inputs.nixpkgs
```
## What it does
Checks for URI expressions that are not quoted.

## Why is this bad?
The Nix language has a special syntax for URLs even though quoted
strings can also be used to represent them. Unlike paths, URLs do
not have any special properties in the Nix expression language
that would make the difference useful. Moreover, using variable
expansion in URLs requires some URLs to be quoted strings anyway.
So the most consistent approach is to always use quoted strings to
represent URLs. Additionally, a semicolon immediately after the
URL can be mistaken for a part of URL by language-agnostic tools
such as terminal emulators.

See RFC 00045 [1] for more.

[1]: https://github.com/NixOS/rfcs/blob/master/rfcs/0045-deprecate-url-syntax.md

## Example

```nix
inputs = {
  gitignore.url = github:hercules-ci/gitignore.nix;
}
```

Quote the URI expression:

```nix
inputs = {
  gitignore.url = "github:hercules-ci/gitignore.nix";
}
```
## What it does
Checks for empty inherit statements.

## Why is this bad?
Useless code, probably the result of a refactor.

## Example

```nix
inherit;
```

Remove it altogether.
## What it does
Checks for usage of the `toPath` function.

## Why is this bad?
`toPath` is deprecated.

## Example

```nix
builtins.toPath "/path"
```

Try these instead:

```nix
# to convert the string to an absolute path:
/. + "/path"
# => /abc

# to convert the string to a path relative to the current directory:
./. + "/bin"
# => /home/np/statix/bin
```
## What it does
Checks for boolean expressions that can be simplified.

## Why is this bad?
Complex booleans affect readibility.

## Example
```nix
if !(x == y) then 0 else 1
```

Use `!=` instead:

```nix
if x != y then 0 else 1
```
## What it does
Checks for expressions that use the "has attribute" operator: `?`,
where the `or` operator would suffice.

## Why is this bad?
The `or` operator is more readable.

## Example
```nix
if x ? a then x.a else some_default
```

Use `or` instead:

```nix
x.a or some_default
```
## What it does
Checks for keys in attribute sets with repetitive keys, and suggests using
an attribute set instead.

## Why is this bad?
Avoiding repetetion helps improve readibility.

## Example
```nix
{
  foo.a = 1;
  foo.b = 2;
  foo.c = 3;
}
```

Don't repeat.
```nix
{
  foo = {
    a = 1;
    b = 2;
    c = 3;
  };
}
```
## What it does
Checks for concatenations to empty lists

## Why is this bad?
Concatenation with the empty list is a no-op.

## Example
```nix
[] ++ something
```

Remove the operation:

```nix
something

architecture
============

statix has the following components:
  * bin: the CLI/entrypoint
  * lib: library of lints and utilities to define these lints
  * vfs: virtual filesystem
  * macros: procedural macros to help define a lint


bin
---

This is the main point of interaction between `statix` and
the end user. It's output is human-readable and should also
support JSON/errorfmt outputs for external tools to use.


lib
---

A library of AST-based lints and utilities to help write
those lints. It should be easy for newcomers to write lints
without being familiar with the rest of the codebase.


vfs
---

VFS is an in-memory filesystem. It provides cheap-to-copy
handles (`FileId`s) to access paths and file contents.


macros
------

This crate intends to be a helper layer to declare lints and
their metadata.
VFS
---
- do all the IO in one place
- pass file handles around

Interface
---------
- load files to be read as VFS
- path interner
- traits to go from Report to text/errfmt
- offline documentation/explaination for lints

Fix
---
- multipass runner with hare & tortoise for cycle detection
- fix all possible suggestions
- work with a config generated by CLI
- read data from VFS
- produce a Report

Analysis
--------
- work with a config generated by CLI
- read data from VFS
- produce a Report

Tests
-----
- figure out a way to generate stable singleline output for
  analysis tests
- use stderr tests for fixes

Lint ideas
----------
- unused let bindings
- unused rec
- invalid or potentially risky string interpolations
- useless parens in infix exprs
- unused function params
- manual map over list
- merge inherit
- merge inherit-from
- empty inherit
- useless antiquote/splice (where is antiquote truly
  required?)
- useless variadic (things like `{...} : expr`, replace with
  `_: expr`)
- redundant pattern `{...} @ inputs : expr`, replace with
  `inputs: expr`
- useless hasAttr: `if x ? a then x.a else default` can be
  replaced with `x.a or default`

Extensions
----------
- vim plugin to populate location list with errors

cd /tmp/cfgdefault && /workspace/executable check -o errfmt .; echo $?
cd /tmp/cfgdefault && /workspace/executable check -o errfmt file.nix; echo $?

# Config with disabled = [] and ignore = ['.direnv'] is default dump output
# Need to test dump always same?
/workspace/executable dump

# Fix for W17 has no fix (empty diff earlier). Let's confirm
cat /tmp/lints/W17.nix | /workspace/executable fix --stdin
/workspace/executable fix --dry-run /tmp/lints/W17.nix

# So some lints have no auto-fix

  echo "CHECK:"
  /workspace/executable check -o errfmt "$f"
  echo "FIX:"
  /workspace/executable fix --dry-run "$f"
  echo "---"
done

# Let's map codes: list gave W03 manual_inherit, so disabling by "manual_inherit" should disable W03. And it did! When we set disabled = ["manual_inherit"], exit 0, meaning W03 was disabled.

# But disabled = ["W03"] did NOT disable W03. So perhaps disabled expects lint name, not code? Let's test more.

cat <<'NIX' > /tmp/c.nix

NIX

for code in W01 W02 W03 W04 W05 W06 W07 W08 W10 W11 W12 W14 W17 W18 W19 W20 W23; do

  echo "Testing disabling code $code name $name"
  cat <<TOML > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = ["$code"]
TOML
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/c.nix 2>&1 | head
  echo -n "with code: exit "
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/c.nix; echo $?
  cat <<TOML > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = ["$name"]

cd /workspace
# Major discovery!

# Config disabled = ["manual_inherit"] EXIT 0  -> disabling by name works
# Config disabled = ["W03", "manual_inherit"] EXIT 0 -> also works because one of them matches manual_inherit
# But disabled = ["W03"] alone still reports W03 -> meaning W03 code does NOT disable manual_inherit? Wait W03 should correspond to manual_inherit.

# Let's map codes: list gave W03 manual_inherit, so disabling by "manual_inherit" should disable W03. And it did! When we set disabled = ["manual_inherit"], exit 0, meaning W03 was disabled.

# But disabled = ["W03"] did NOT disable W03. So perhaps disabled expects lint name, not code? Let's test more.

cat <<'NIX' > /tmp/c.nix
let a = 2; in { a = a; }
NIX

for code in W01 W02 W03 W04 W05 W06 W07 W08 W10 W11 W12 W14 W17 W18 W19 W20 W23; do
  # find name
  name=$(/workspace/executable list | grep "^$code" | awk '{print $2}')
  echo "Testing disabling code $code name $name"
  cat <<TOML > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = ["$code"]
TOML
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/c.nix 2>&1 | head
  echo -n "with code: exit "
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/c.nix; echo $?
  cat <<TOML > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = ["$name"]
TOML
  echo -n "with name: exit "
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/c.nix; echo $?
  echo "---"
done

# Test W01 with its file
cat <<'NIX' > /tmp/W01.nix
if x == true then 0 else 1
NIX
for dis in "W01" "bool_comparison"; do
  cat <<TOML > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = ["$dis"]
TOML
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/W01.nix; echo "disabled $dis exit $?"
done

# So disabled expects lint NAME not CODE. Let's verify with all lints
for f in /tmp/lints/*.nix; do
  base=$(basename $f .nix)
  # base is W01 etc
  name=$(/workspace/executable list | grep "^$base" | awk '{print $2}')
  echo "=== $base ($name) ==="
  cat <<TOML > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = ["$base"]
TOML
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt "$f"; echo "disable code $base exit $?"
  cat <<TOML > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = ["$name"]
TOML
  /workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt "$f"; echo "disable name $name exit $?"
done

# What about ignore field? Earlier test showed ignore = ["c.nix"] didn't ignore when target is file directly. Let's test ignore with directory target
mkdir -p /tmp/igntest
echo 'let a=2; in { a=a; }' > /tmp/igntest/a.nix
echo 'let a=2; in { a=a; }' > /tmp/igntest/b.nix

cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = []
ignore = ["a.nix"]
TOML
/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/igntest; echo exit:$?
/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/igntest/a.nix; echo exit:$?

cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = []
ignore = ["b.nix"]
TOML
/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/igntest; echo exit:$?

cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/cfgtest/statix.toml
disabled = []
ignore = ["*.nix"]
TOML
/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/cfgtest -o errfmt /tmp/igntest; echo exit:$?

# Default ignore .direnv: we saw earlier default check did NOT ignore .direnv when checking /tmp/testdir - it reported both files. That suggests default ignore only applies if config file exists? Or maybe .direnv ignore only applies when config file's ignore includes it, but dump's ignore is sample config, not default built-in? Let's check docs/architecture perhaps mentions ignore.

# Dump output says disabled = [] ignore = ['.direnv'] - that is sample config. So default behavior when no config file is to NOT ignore .direnv? But earlier we thought it should ignore .direnv by default. Let's test again more carefully.

mkdir -p /tmp/testdir/.direnv
echo 'let a=2; in { a=a; }' > /tmp/testdir/.direnv/file.nix
echo 'let a=2; in { a=a; }' > /tmp/testdir/file.nix
rm -f /tmp/testdir/statix.toml
/workspace/executable check -o errfmt /tmp/testdir; echo exit:$?
# Now create config with ignore = ['.direnv']
cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/testdir/statix.toml
disabled = []
ignore = [".direnv"]
TOML
/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/testdir -o errfmt /tmp/testdir; echo exit:$?
cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/testdir/statix.toml
disabled = []
ignore = [".direnv/file.nix"]
TOML
/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/testdir -o errfmt /tmp/testdir; echo exit:$?
cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/testdir/statix.toml
disabled = []
ignore = [".direnv/*"]
TOML
/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/testdir -o errfmt /tmp/testdir; echo exit:$?

/workspace/executable check -o errfmt /tmp/testdir -i ".direnv/*"; echo exit:$?
/workspace/executable check -o errfmt /tmp/testdir -i ".direnv/file.nix"; echo exit:$?

# Now test .gitignore handling again with config ignore
mkdir -p /tmp/gittest2
cd /tmp/gittest2

echo 'let a=2; in { a=a; }' > file.nix
echo 'let a=2; in { a=a; }' > file.log
/workspace/executable check -o errfmt .; echo exit:$?
/workspace/executable check -u -o errfmt .; echo exit:$?
rm -rf /tmp/gittest2

echo 'let a=2; in { a=a; }' > /tmp/fixtest2/b.nix
cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/fixtest2/statix.toml
disabled = ["manual_inherit"]
TOML

/workspace/executable check --config /tmp/fixtest2 -o errfmt /tmp/fixtest2; echo exit:$?
cat <<'TOML' > /tmp/fixtest2/statix.toml
disabled = []
ignore = ["a.nix"]
TOML
/workspace/executable fix --dry-run --config /tmp/fixtest2 /tmp/fixtest2; echo exit:$?

# statix

> Lints and suggestions for the Nix programming language.

`statix check` highlights antipatterns in Nix code. `statix
fix` can fix several such occurrences.

For the time-being, `statix` works only with ASTs
produced by the `rnix-parser` crate and does not evaluate
any nix code (imports, attr sets etc.).

## Examples

```shell
$ statix check tests/c.nix
[W04] Warning: Assignment instead of inherit from
   ╭─[tests/c.nix:2:3]
   │
 2 │   mtl = pkgs.haskellPackages.mtl;
   ·   ───────────────┬───────────────
   ·                  ╰───────────────── This assignment is better written with inherit
───╯

$ statix fix --dry-run tests/c.nix
--- tests/c.nix
+++ tests/c.nix [fixed]
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 let
-  mtl = pkgs.haskellPackages.mtl;
+  inherit (pkgs.haskellPackages) mtl;
 in
 null
```

## Installation

`statix` is available via a nix flake:

name = "statix"

clap = "4.6.1"
glob = "0.3"

ignore = "0.4"
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
toml = "1.1.2"
